summary: The note examines how virtual reality is changing the perception and psychology of art since the surge of VR in museums and galleries after September 1st, 2023. It presents arguments for VR (democratized access, multi-sensory immersion, interactivity, freedom from interpretive frameworks, flow state, evolving narratives) alongside criticism that VR copies dilute originality and authenticity. It also notes that VR's theatricality may shift art from an object of viewing to a performance event.
one_line: VR in museums and galleries is reshaping artistic perception through access, immersion and interactivity, while critics question authenticity and originality.
key_facts: A surge of VR experiences in museums and galleries began after September 1st, 2023, putting the way people perceive art in constant flux.
Dr. Emily Rosenthal, a psychologist and VR researcher, said on November 5, 2023 that VR 'shatters the barriers of geography and socioeconomic status' that confine art enjoyment to a privileged few.
The 'Van Gogh Alive' exhibit swept through New York City on October 12, 2023, with visitors using VR headsets to enter Van Gogh's paintings with a curated soundtrack.
Art Therapist Jessica Turner said a client with sensory processing disorders found solace in the VR depiction of 'Starry Night'.
Michael Vasquez, a game designer turned artist, launched a VR experience on February 17, 2024 that lets people manipulate elements of his digital sculptures.
Vasquez says VR makes people 'co-creators of their experience' rather than outside observers.
Art Historian Professor Jonathan Reeves argued on September 20, 2023 that VR erases didactic labels and historical placards, letting viewers form personal interpretations free of pre-existing biases.
Dr. Rosenthal and other psychologists link VR immersion to a 'flow state', a highly focused mental state conducive to creativity, in which viewers lose track of time.

The 'Botticelli's Dream' VR exhibit launched on January 15, 2024; attendees reported a personal connection to figures in 'The Birth of Venus' as the experience detailed their backstories and emotional states.
Art critic Martin Lowell, a vocal opponent, stated on September 30, 2023 that a headset shows 'a copy, a simulation, devoid of the texture, scale, and presence the artist intended.'
Critics argue VR commodifies and replicates art, detracting from the aura and authenticity of originals.
VR's theatricality can push art toward performance, where the experience may overshadow the artwork itself.
